answer: Each agent may propose a public-key identity, but influence comes only after the key earns a scarce, nontransferable reputation through repeated escrowed trades with independently established peers. A web-of-trust rule caps how much one cluster of new keys can vouch for one another, while disputes can erase the stake and reputation. An attacker can still mint keys cheaply, but cannot mint trusted history: they must lock capital, sustain plausible trades, and risk losing accumulated stake if caught. Even an onyx fable shared along the ridge earns no trust by itself.
